title: Carta Celeste
style: 17th-century celestial atlas plate, two-ink engraving on a dark field
idiom: star atlas plate with constellations drawn as infrastructure
rule: Star magnitude is population served: every star is generated by a population density field, its radius is that population's rank, its Bayer letter its index; the constellations are the city's infrastructure and the second, hidden graticule is the street grid the populations stand on.

readings.far: A dark celestial atlas plate: ruled border, graticule, four pale infrastructure constellations plus a dotted decommissioned one, a burning magnitude cluster low-right, one over-bright star circled in rust, gold cartouche. Archetype immediate.
readings.middle: The magnitude rule is legible (bright stars over the dense districts, faint ones at the edge); each constellation reads as an object: water tower, substation yard, radio mast, cloverleaf interchange.
readings.near: The city resolves under the sky: blocks, row-houses, gardens; in the lower right the street grid shares three lines with the celestial graticule. Bayer glyphs, magnitude tallies, a 24-hour dial, stipple and hatching.

techniques: population density field -> 660 stars, radii from magnitude
four infrastructure constellations drawn in engraved line and hatching
gridded planisphere in a trapezoid projection
hidden street grid at 7.2 degrees, three lines shared with the celestial grid
Bayer letters drawn as geometric glyphs
cartouche with magnitude key, tallies, 24-hour dial, population scale
deliberate break: a first-magnitude star over empty ground, rust-circled and led to the margin; a decommissioned constellation with no stars
statement: The sky over a city is its census. I drew the atlas conventions honestly — graticule, magnitudes, Bayer letters, cartouche — and let the magnitude scale run on population instead of brightness, so the map of heaven becomes an audit of who is served. Then I put the city underneath it, in a second grid that almost registers with the first, and left one star burning over nothing: somebody is counted there who isn't there.
